extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, USPTO OED staff, and attorneys who practice before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and rules governing practitioner conduct before the USPTO (communication, neglect, withdrawal, and related disciplinary obligations), as applied in enforcement/disciplinary proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) — Disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules provide at 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a) that a 'practitioner shall not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct,' which is defined at § 10.23(b)(1) as including '[v]iolat[ing] a disciplinary rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a high-level prohibition; specific examples of conduct that constitute disreputable or gross misconduct are listed in § 10.23(c). Violations of disciplinary rules (e.g., neglect, failure to communicate) fall within disreputable/gross misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(8) — Failing to inform client of Office correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to inform a client or former client . . . of correspondence received from the Office . . . when the correspondence (i) could have a significant effect on a matter pending before the Office, (ii) is received by the practitioner on behalf of a client or former client and (iii) is correspondence of which a reasonable practitioner would believe under the circumstances the client or former client should be notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specific example of disreputable/gross misconduct applies where Office mailings (e.g., Notices to File Missing Parts, Office Actions, Notices of Abandonment) could significantly affect prosecution. The practitioner's duty includes notifying clients of such correspondence when a reasonable practitioner would do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c) — Neglect of a legal matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In 37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c), the Rules state that a 'practitioner shall not . . . [n]eglect a legal matter entrusted to the practitioner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect includes failing to respond to Office actions or other filings necessary to preserve a client's patent rights. The Director used this as the basis for alleging abandonment of clients' applications due to practitioner inaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(1) — Fail to seek lawful objectives of a client
rubrics_metrics.description: As stated in 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a), the Rules provide that in representing a client, a 'practitioner shall not intentionally: (1) Fail to seek the lawful objectives of a client through reasonably available means permitted by law and the Disciplinary Rules.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to patent prosecution, this requires using reasonably available procedural and substantive means to pursue a client's goals (e.g., making necessary responses to Office communications) unless barred by law or disciplinary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(2) — Fail to carry out a contract of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(2): 'Fail to carry out a contract of employment entered into with a client for professional services, but a practitioner may withdraw as permitted under §§ 10.40, 10.63, and 10.66.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner who agreed to provide patent prosecution services must carry them out unless properly withdrawing. If charging/nonpayment is the issue, the practitioner should seek permitted withdrawal rather than simply ceasing work; case law cited indicates failure to carry out agreed services can be disciplinary even if unpaid.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(3) — Prejudice or damage to a client
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(3): 'Prejudice or damage a client during the course of a professional relationship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional actions or omissions that damage a client's interests (for example, allowing applications to become abandoned) can violate this subsection. The standard looks to whether client rights were prejudiced or damaged by the practitioner's conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 10.40 — Withdrawal from employment before the Office
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not withdraw from employment in a proceeding before the Office without permission from the Office . . . . In any event, a practitioner shall not withdraw from employment until the practitioner has taken reasonable steps to avoid foreseeable prejudice to the rights of the client, including giving due notice to his or her client, allowing time for employment of another practitioner, delivering to the client all papers and property to which the client is entitled, and complying with all applicable laws and rules. A practitioner who withdraws from employment shall refund promptly any part of a fee paid in advance that has not been earned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ceasing representation in a prosecution matter a practitioner must either obtain Office permission to withdraw (where required) or take the listed reasonable steps to avoid prejudice — notice, time to secure successor counsel, returning client papers, compliance with rules, prompt refund of unearned fees. Simply stopping work without notice/steps can be disciplinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)–(b) — Communication and explanation duties
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a): A practitioner shall: (1) Promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance with respect to which the client’s informed consent is required by the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct; (2) Reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client’s objectives are to be accomplished; (3) Keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter; (4) Promptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client; and (5) Consult with the client about any relevant limitation on the practitioner’s conduct when the practitioner knows that the client expects assistance not permitted by the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct or other law. (b) A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parallel to ABA Model Rule 1.4 requires timely status communications, consultation about strategy and means, prompt responses to client information requests, advising when client expectations exceed permissible conduct, and explaining matters sufficiently for informed client decisions. Failure to keep clients reasonably informed or to respond promptly supports disciplinary findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival of abandoned application requires showing abandonment was unintentional
rubrics_metrics.description: Revival of an abandoned patent application generally requires a showing that the abandonment was unintentional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioner neglect that results in abandonment can be particularly prejudicial because revival typically requires demonstrating unintentional delay — making failure to notify or to respond more serious in impact on client rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of time-extension purchases under 37 C.F.R. / 7 C.F.R. § 1.136(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office Action provided that extensions of time of up to five months were available for purchase under 7 C.F.R. § 1.136(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Office Actions set short response windows, practitioners may have the option to purchase time extensions (where applicable); failure to consider/purchase available extensions may contribute to neglect/abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiduciary duty owed even if client unpaid (case law principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director argued that Respondent had a fiduciary duty to Mr. Openiano to protect his intellectual property rights, whether he paid Respondent or not, citing Atilus v. United States, 406 F.2d 694, 696 (5th Cir. 1969).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant authority supports that an attorney retained to represent a client owes duties of representation even where payment is not made; nonpayment does not automatically excuse neglect or failure to notify the client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on double-counting under § 10.23(b)(6) / § 11.804(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Complaint also alleged violations of 37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6) and the analogous provision in Part 11, 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i), because he engaged in 'other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner’s fitness to practice before the Office.' However, the Director did not discuss those subsections in the Post Hearing Brief. The PTO’s appellate tribunal has held that 'to be 'other' conduct within the scope [of] Section 10.23(b)(6), conduct must not be prohibited by Section 10.23(b)(1)–(5).' Accordingly, Respondent cannot be found to have violated both subsection 10.23(b)(6) and another subsection of 10.23(b), or both subsection 11.804(i) and another subsection of 11.804.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretative limitation: 'other' conduct provisions are mutually exclusive of specifically enumerated misconduct subsections; analysts/adjudicators should avoid charging the same factual conduct under both an enumerated subsection and the 'other' subsection.
